tldr: When transferring human hand-object interactions to dexterous robot hands in physics simulation (retargeting), instead of training a separate policy for each video clip, this paper proposes learning multiple motions simultaneously with a single reinforcement learning policy. The method achieves a ~2.5x higher success rate (90%) with roughly 100x less training compute compared to prior RL baselines, and also demonstrates successful transfer to a real robot.

A single policy accurately reproduces complex motions across vastly different geometries and hand-object contact patterns, including tool use, container handling, and grasping everyday objects.
overview:
Learning dexterous robot manipulation policies requires massive amounts of robot interaction data. A promising approach is "physics-based retargeting," which translates recordings (datasets) of human hand-object interactions directly onto robot embodiments. However, existing methods suffer from severe bottlenecks. Sampling-based trajectory optimization methods struggle with wide search spaces and suffer low success rates, while reinforcement learning (RL) methods achieve higher precision but train a policy from scratch for each single reference motion, causing compute costs to scale linearly with dataset size.

To address this, the authors asked: "Can we train a single policy across many motions (multi-reference tracking) to share experience and dramatically amortize training compute?" In dexterous manipulation, however, object shapes and contact relationships vary wildly across motions, and human motion capture data contains geometric contact artifacts, so simply training on all motions together fails. To overcome these hurdles, the authors built "FlashDexRetarget," a framework combining point-cloud observations that capture object geometry, continuous hand-object distance rewards, future trajectory encodings, separate left- and right-hand actor-critic architectures, and buffer/model extensions to the off-policy RL algorithm FlashSAC.

In experiments across a 50-motion benchmark, FlashDexRetarget achieved a 90% success rate—roughly 44 percentage points higher than the leading RL-based baseline CHORD—while requiring approximately 100x less GPU compute. The authors also showed that motion generation remains stable and increasingly efficient when scaling up to 1,000 motions, and they successfully replayed the retargeted motions on real robot hardware.
contributions: Proposed a multi-reference learning framework that retargets multiple human hand-object motions simultaneously using a single reinforcement learning policy.
Combined object point-cloud observations, future trajectory encodings, and continuous distance-based rewards robust to imperfect contact data to adapt across diverse geometric relationships.
Significantly boosted learning efficiency and representation capacity through separate left- and right-hand actor-critic networks and extensions to large-scale off-policy RL (FlashSAC).
Achieved a 90% success rate on a 50-motion benchmark using ~1/100 of the compute of prior RL baselines, while validating scalability up to 1,000 motions and successful playback on real hardware.

sections.heading: Training one by one is over: Tackling multi-reference tracking across diverse motions
sections.summary: Existing physics-based retargeting of human dexterous data requires separate optimization or training per motion, scaling compute costs linearly. FlashDexRetarget proposes tracking multiple motions concurrently with a single policy, cutting compute by 100x while substantially increasing retargeting success.
sections.details:
Developing dexterous multi-fingered manipulation requires vast amounts of data, but collecting it via direct robot teleoperation is extremely demanding. Consequently, researchers have turned to physics-based retargeting, taking motion-captured human hand-object datasets and adapting them to robot kinematics and physical contacts inside simulation.

However, existing physics-based retargeting faces major issues. Sampling-based trajectory optimization struggles to navigate high-dimensional joint spaces and long contact sequences, hitting a ceiling in success rate under finite time budgets. Meanwhile, recent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches offer high contact fidelity, but they rely on a single-reference setup where an individual policy is trained from scratch for every single clip, requiring thousands of GPU hours to process an entire dataset.

In humanoid whole-body locomotion, multi-reference tracking—following various walking and running motions with a single policy—has shown great success. But directly applying this to dexterous hand-object manipulation runs into unique challenges:

- Object geometries and grasp configurations differ across every clip, requiring the policy to distinguish geometric relationships
- Motion capture data of humans includes contact gaps and mesh penetrations, making exact contact matching unreliable
- Tracking diverse motions simultaneously broadens the state distribution, making model capacity and efficient replay buffer reuse essential
- Bimanual manipulation assigns asymmetric roles to the hands (e.g., one hand stabilizes while the other unscrews)

FlashDexRetarget overcomes these hurdles by combining geometric and future-trajectory observation designs, distance-based interaction rewards, separate left/right networks, and off-policy RL extensions. As a result, it cuts compute by around 100x compared to RL baselines like CHORD while boosting benchmark success rates from 46% to 90%.

sections.heading: Limits of geometric transfer and the bottleneck of single-motion physics baselines
sections.summary: Transferring human hand data to robots generally relies on either kinematic IK-based methods or physics-based methods that account for contacts. Kinematic methods cannot guarantee real physical contact, while prior physics-based methods optimize motions independently, limiting computational efficiency.
sections.details:
### II-A Human Hand-Object Interaction Data
Recent advances in computer vision have yielded numerous high-fidelity 3D datasets of human hand-object interactions, such as DexYCB, GRAB, OakInk, HOT3D, TACO, and OakInk2. However, these are recorded based on human hand skeletons (e.g., MANO models) and cannot be executed directly on robotic hands.

Early retargeting approaches like UniDex and VideoManip adopted kinematic retargeting, aligning fingertips to object surfaces via inverse kinematics (IK) or keypoint matching. However, these methods only align positions geometrically without simulating physical contact forces applied to objects. Consequently, when executed on a real robot, objects often slip or fail to follow the intended motion. Physics-based retargeting that considers contact dynamics is therefore indispensable.

### II-B Dexterous Physics-Based Retargeting from Human Motion
Physics-based retargeting falls into two main camps: sampling-based and RL-based.
Sampling-based methods like SPIDER and Do as I Do search for control sequences via rollouts in simulation. However, they require a separate search for every single motion clip, heavily depend on initialization and reference quality, and struggle to find stable long-horizon trajectories amid dexterous multi-contact local optima.

On the other hand, RL-based methods such as ManipTrans, DexMachina, and CHORD learn high-accuracy tracking policies using contact forces and auxiliary guidance. Yet, they still train one dedicated policy per reference motion, scaling compute costs linearly with dataset size. FlashDexRetarget breaks free from this limitation by learning across multiple motions simultaneously, amortizing training compute across the entire dataset.

sections.heading: The full FlashDexRetarget design: Geometry-aware, forward-looking, dual-hand, and off-policy RL
sections.summary: To track multiple motions with a single policy, observations incorporate wrist-relative point clouds, distance features, and a 10-step future trajectory window. The method also introduces signed distance field (SDF) rewards that avoid rigid contact labels, independent actor-critics for each hand, and a scaled-up off-policy RL engine (FlashSAC).
sections.details:
### III-A Observation Space Design (Geometry Awareness & Future Conditioning)
Handling multiple distinct motions with a single policy requires telling the network exactly which object it is interacting with and how:

- **Interaction-Aware Observations**: To represent object shape, 128 sampled object surface points are transformed into the wrist's local coordinate frame at both the current step and the next target step ($\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cur}}_{t}$, $\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{i,t+1}$). Using the wrist frame preserves invariance across relative hand-object configurations. Additionally, a local distance feature vector $\mathbf{d}^{\mathrm{cur}}_{t}$ concatenates distances and surface normals from each fingertip and the wrist to the object surface.
- **Future Reference Frame Conditioning**: Most existing methods only look one step ahead. In contrast, FlashDexRetarget encodes hand and object trajectories from the next step up to $K=10$ steps ahead using a temporal encoder $\mathrm{Enc}_{\psi}$, providing a 128-dimensional latent vector to the policy. This lookahead allows the hand to anticipate upcoming interaction phases and pre-shape effectively.

### III-B Reward Design (Point Cloud Tracking & Continuous Distance)
- **Point-Cloud Object Tracking Reward**: Separately tuning translation and rotation error weights is difficult. Instead, the authors measure displacement across 128 surface points normalized to a sphere of radius $\rho=0.058\,\mathrm{m}$. Rather than taking the overall mean, the reward averages the top 3 largest point errors, heavily penalizing large object misalignments.
- **Hand-Object Interaction Reward**: Human capture data often contains millimeter-level penetrations or contact gaps, making binary contact classification a poor RL signal. Instead, the framework computes fingertip-to-object distances using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and applies a smooth, continuous penalty only when the robot's hand-object distance exceeds that of the human reference.

### III-C Decoupled Bimanual Architecture
Controlling both hands with a single actor-critic collapses both hands' contributions into a single scalar reward, destabilizing training in asymmetric tasks (e.g., holding an object with one hand while unscrewing with the other). The proposed architecture assigns separate actors $\pi_{\theta_h}$ and critics $Q_{\phi_h}$ to the left and right hands. They share full-state observations, but decouple action outputs and learning signals (rewards).

### III-D Scaled Off-Policy RL
Because multi-reference learning spans diverse state transitions, sample-efficient off-policy RL is crucial. The framework adopts FlashSAC, expanding the replay buffer from the standard 10M to 50M transitions and widening the critic hidden layer dimension from 256 to 1024 to substantially enhance representation capacity.

sections.heading: Dramatic efficiency and high success: 100x compute savings and scaling to 1,000 motions
sections.summary: On a 50-motion benchmark, FlashDexRetarget achieved a ~44% higher success rate than prior work (CHORD) with approximately 100x less GPU compute. Ablations validated each design choice, while further experiments proved scalability up to 1,000 motions and successful replay on physical hardware.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The benchmark comprises 50 diverse interaction motions selected from TACO, OakInk2, and HOT3D (25 single-object and 25 two-object tasks). Evaluated hands include the 5-finger XHand and the 4-finger Sharpa Wave Hand in IsaacSim. Metrics include object pose success rate $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{MT\text{-}Obj}}$, a stricter metric including joint and fingertip errors $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{MT}}$, and the widely used $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{SPIDER}}$.

### IV-B Retargeting Performance and Efficiency (RQ1)
On XHand, FlashDexRetarget achieved a 90% success rate on $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{SPIDER}}$. In contrast, sampling-based Do as I Do reached 36% (using ~60 GPU hours), and RL-based CHORD reached 46% (using ~3,000 GPU hours). FlashDexRetarget reached 90% in only about 30 GPU hours—yielding roughly double the success rate of CHORD with ~100x less compute. Under the stricter $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{MT}}$ metric requiring precise hand tracking, baselines scored between 0% and 12%, whereas FlashDexRetarget retained an 86% success rate. Similar gains were observed on the Sharpa Wave Hand.

### IV-C Component Ablations (RQ2)
- **Future Trajectory Input**: Removing the $K=10$ lookahead slowed down the accumulation rate of successful trajectories, showing that future awareness helps pre-shape for contacts.
- **Point Clouds and Contact Rewards**: Omitting point cloud observations and rewards caused a steep drop in success rate, while removing distance interaction rewards slowed learning considerably. Removing both yielded the worst performance.
- **Decoupled Hand Architecture**: Compared to a Unified Actor-Critic, the decoupled setup learned significantly more motions at a faster pace.
- **Off-Policy RL and Capacity**: PPO achieved near 0% success under a 300M environment step budget. Switching to baseline FlashSAC reached 34%, and scaling both buffer size (50M) and critic width (1024) achieved peak performance.

### IV-D Scaling to Large Motion Sets (RQ3)
The authors scaled training sets to 200, 500, and 1,000 reference clips. Within the same step budget, larger reference sets yielded a higher absolute count of successfully retargeted clips, proving that multi-reference tracking effectively shares knowledge and amortizes learning costs.

### IV-E Real-World Execution (RQ4)
Retargeted trajectories from simulation were directly replayed on a physical robot arm-hand setup across three tasks: board wiping, pouring beans into a pan, and closing a bottle cap. All tasks were executed successfully in the real world.

Each element directly drives learning speed and final retargeting success.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: Paving the way for large-scale data generation
sections.summary: FlashDexRetarget dramatically boosts the efficiency and success rate of dexterous robot data generation via multi-reference tracking RL. While currently reliant on high-quality 3D capture data, future work aims for direct retargeting from monocular video and zero-shot generalization.
sections.details:
This work introduced FlashDexRetarget, a framework that converts large collections of human hand-object interactions into dexterous robot motions using a single reference-conditioned RL policy. By uniting geometry- and contact-aware observations and rewards, decoupled bimanual networks, and scaled off-policy RL, it achieves a 90% retargeting success rate at 100x lower compute than prior baselines. Scaling experiments also demonstrated that multi-reference learning becomes increasingly cost-effective as the dataset grows.

The authors also outline several limitations. The current framework assumes relatively clean 3D hand-object tracking data, accurate 3D CAD models, and privileged contact information inside simulation. Key avenues for future work include developing robust front-end pipelines to retarget directly from in-the-wild videos, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen motions or robot embodiments, and distilling successful trajectories into vision-based autonomous closed-loop student policies.

takeaways: Switching from training a separate RL policy per motion to a single multi-reference policy dramatically amortizes computational cost.
When retargeting imperfect human motion data, continuous distance penalties from Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) work far better than discrete contact labels.
In multi-motion tracking setups, off-policy RL (such as FlashSAC) equipped with large replay buffers and wide critic networks overwhelmingly outperforms on-policy methods like PPO.
For bimanual manipulation, decoupling action spaces and learning signals (rewards) per hand is critical for managing asymmetric hand roles.
limitations: Requires accurate 3D object meshes and clean human hand tracking data as input, requiring pre-processing pipelines before working directly on noisy RGB video.

Trains using privileged simulation state information (accurate SDFs and point clouds), requiring distillation (e.g., student-teacher setups) before deployment as autonomous closed-loop policies in the real world.
Evaluation metrics focus primarily on joint and object pose errors, without fully evaluating functional task objectives (e.g., whether liquid actually spilled).
